--- title: "Take-home Exercise 02: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good - Urban mobility" author: "Yiqiong PAN" date: "Oct 1, 2025" date-modified: last-modified execute: echo: true # display the code eval: true # run the code message: false warning: false freeze: true # do not re-render if nothing edited format: html: toc: true code-link: true number-sections: true number-depth: 4 editor: visual --- ## Overview ### Background and Motivation Urban mobility refers to the movement of people and goods across all transport modes within and between cities. With population growth and climate pressures, cities are developing smart and sustainable transport systems to enhance liveability and reduce emissions. Digitalised infrastructures such as buses, MRT, and roads now generate vast datasets from technologies like smart cards, GPS, and RFID. For instance, the tap-on and tap-off data from smart cards capture not only trip origins but also destinations, enabling analysis of passenger flow and discount points. Yet, such data are often used only for simple GIS mapping, rather than deeper spatial or spatio-temporal analysis that could uncover richer mobility insights. ### Methods & Objective **Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA)** identify specific locations where values are significantly clustered or dispersed. Unlike global measures that summarise the whole map, LMSA tests each location to detect hotspots (high-value clusters), cold spots (low-value clusters), and spatial outliers. **Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)** extends LMSA into the spatio-temporal domain, using a space–time cube to reveal how hot and cold spots evolve over time. By combining local Gi* statistics with the Mann–Kendall trend test, EHSA classifies patterns as new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic. Using LTA’s Passenger Volume data and an analytical hexagon grid of 375 m, this exercise analyses passenger trips generated by origin at the hexagon level during **three** peak periods: - weekday morning (6 am – 9 am), - weekday afternoon (5 pm – 8 pm), - weekend/holiday (11 am – 8 pm); to uncover neighbourhood-level mobility variations and emerging commuting trends for more responsive transport planning. ## Loading Packages in to R There are **six** packages used in this exercise. `add more package` | Package | Description | |-----------------------|------------------------------------------------| | [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) | Handles importing, managing, and processing vector-based geospatial data | | [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) | A collection of R packages for data wrangling and visualisation, including **readr**, **dplyr**, and **ggplot2**. | | [tmap](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/) | Creates cartographic quality static and interactive thematic (choropleth) maps. | | [knitr](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/knitr/index.html/) | Provides an elegant, flexible, and fast static table generation with R | | [kableExtra](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kableExtra/vignettes/awesome_table_in_html.html) | An extension of knitr for creating elegant html table with R | | [DT](https://rstudio.github.io/DT/) | Provides an R interface to the JavaScript library DataTables for create interactive htnl tables. | | [rvest](https://rvest.tidyverse.org/) | Scrapes or harvests data from web pages. | : {tbl-colwidths="\[15,85\]"} The code chunk below loads the required package into R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, sfdep, tmap, knitr, kableExtra, DT, rvest) ``` ::: ## Getting the Data into R environment 1. Singapore boundary data, that we explored in Hands-on Ex 1-2 2. LTADataMall: bus stop locations in SHP 3. LTADataMall: the bus trip data for August 2025 were retrieved using GetPostman to download the CSV file. ### Importing the Geospatial Ploygon Data: Master Plan 2019 Subzone The code chunk below imports Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) from Singapore’s open data portal. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source `C:\lsrgc\ISSS626-yiqiong-pan\Take-home_Ex\Take-home_Ex02\data\geospatial\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml' using driver `KML' Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775 Geodetic CRS: WGS 84 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) { # return NA if missing or empty if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_) page <- read_html(html_text) #parse the HTML string rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr") #get all table rows value <- rows %>% keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>% #keep row where table header text = field_name html_element("td") %>% #take its table data html_text2() #extract clean text if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value #return NA if no match, otherwise the value } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mpsz <- mpsz %>% mutate( #for each description string, call the function, It returns a length-1 character per row (or NA) REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"), PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"), SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"), SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C") ) %>% select(-Name, -Description) %>% #drop the raw KML attributes relocate(geometry, .after = last_col()) #move the geometry column to the end ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(mpsz) ``` ::: Reading layer `BusStop' from data source `C:\lsrgc\ISSS626-yiqiong-pan\Take-home_Ex\Take-home_Ex02\data\LTADataMall' using driver `ESRI Shapefile' Simple feature collection with 5172 features and 2 fields Geometry type: POINT Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 3970.122 ymin: 26482.1 xmax: 48285.52 ymax: 52983.82 Projected CRS: SVY21 ``` ::: ::: ### Importing the Attribute Data: Bus Trips The code chunk below imports *Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops* downloaded from LTA DataMall into R environment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} odbus <- read_csv("data/LTADataMall/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv") summary(odbus) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` YEAR_MONTH DAY_TYPE TIME_PER_HOUR PT_TYPE Length:5876969 Length:5876969 Qu.: 13.00 Max. :34148.00 ``` ::: ::: ### Visualisation of the Bus Stop Distribution in Singapore Here we plot the bus stops in Singapore to see the distribution of their locations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(st_geometry(mpsz)) plot(st_geometry(BusStop), add = TRUE, cex = 0.5, col ="blue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #tmap_mode("view") tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_polygons() + tm_shape(BusStop) + tm_dots() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tmap_mode("plot") ``` ::: Since there are a few points located outside the Singapore boundary, these need to be excluded. If we encounter an error message such as st_crs(x) != st_crs(y), it indicates that the coordinate reference systems (CRS) of the two objects are not the same. In such cases, we should assign the correct and consistent CRS (i.e., EPSG:3414). Both st_transform() and st_set_crs() can be used to apply the appropriate CRS. ### Extracting Bus Stops Located within Singapore The code chunk below uses [`st_join()`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/st_join.html) to select all bus stops within Singapore. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BusStop_in_SG <- st_join( BusStop, mpsz, join = st_within, left = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(duplicated(BusStop_in_SG$BUS_STOP_N)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(BusStop_in_SG) # total rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5167 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(unique(BusStop_in_SG$BUS_STOP_N)) # unique bus stops ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5149 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dp_busstops <-BusStop_in_SG %>% group_by(BUS_STOP_N) %>% filter(n()> 1) %>% arrange(BUS_STOP_N) kable(head(dp_busstops)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |BUS_STOP_N |LOC_DESC |REGION_N |PLN_AREA_N |SUBZONE_N |SUBZONE_C |geometry | |:----------|:-------------------------|:--------------|:-----------|:-------------------|:---------|:-------------------------| |09047 |Orchard Rd |CENTRAL REGION |ORCHARD |BOULEVARD |ORSZ02 |POINT (27966.82 31863.63) | |09047 |ORCHARD STN / TANGS PLAZA |CENTRAL REGION |ORCHARD |BOULEVARD |ORSZ02 |POINT (27934.58 31884.22) | |11009 |Ghim Moh Ter |CENTRAL REGION |QUEENSTOWN |GHIM MOH |QTSZ01 |POINT (23101.34 32594.17) | |11009 |GHIM MOH TER |CENTRAL REGION |QUEENSTOWN |GHIM MOH |QTSZ01 |POINT (23100.58 32604.36) | |22501 |Blk 662A |WEST REGION |JURONG WEST |JURONG WEST CENTRAL |JWSZ09 |POINT (13489.09 35536.4) | |22501 |BLK 662A |WEST REGION |JURONG WEST |JURONG WEST CENTRAL |JWSZ09 |POINT (13488.02 35537.88) | ::: ::: There are **5** bus stops outside of Singapore. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BusStop_SG <- st_join( BusStop, mpsz, join = st_within, left = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(BusStop_SG$BUS_STOP_N) - length(BusStop_in_SG$BUS_STOP_N) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: Next, we double-check that the points have been correctly filtered to include only those within Singapore. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_polygons() + tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) + tm_dots() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Creating the analytical hexagons (Singapore with Honeycomb Grid) - cellsize: A numeric value (length 1 or 2) specifying the target cell size. For square/rectangular cells, this defines width and height. For hexagonal cells, it defines the distance between opposite edges. So for the actual analysis, we should use `cellsize = 750`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz, cellsize = 750, ## attention 375m required for take-home ex. what = "polygon", square = FALSE) %>% st_sf() ## this st_* function doesn't return sf data.frame, we need to specifically coerce the file to sf object. ``` ::: ### Checking the hexagon layer visually The code chunk below creates the hexagon grid with bus stop in Singapore. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: We identified two tasks from the hexagon: 1. In mpsz, the unique IDs SUBZONE_N or SUBZONE_C should be attached to the hexagon geometries. 2. Keep only hexagons that contain at least one bus stop. ## Selecting hexagons with bus stops ### Filtering hexagons with bus stops To implement this, we first filter the hexagons using a spatial intersection with the bus-stop points. Recall: st_intersection() returns the geometric overlap (catchment), while st_intersects() returns a logical relation (TRUE/FALSE). After filtering, the hexagon count is reduced from 4,524 to 924. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon$busstop_count = lengths(st_intersects(hexagon, BusStop_in_SG)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon <- filter(hexagon, busstop_count >0) ``` ::: ### Checking the hexagon layer visually The plot confirms only the hexagon with bus stops retained. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_fill("green",fill_alpha =0.9) + tm_shape(hexagon) + tm_polygons("grey90") + tm_borders("gray60") + tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) + tm_dots("black", size = 0.1,shape = 19) + tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) + tm_scalebar() + tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) + tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & LTADataMall", position = c("right", "bottom")) + tm_title("Analytical Honeycomb Grid with Bus Stops in Singapore", size = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Assigning ids to each hexagon Here we have a quick look the hexagon dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kable(head(hexagon)) %>% kable_styling(font_size = 24) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
geometry busstop_count

````` ::: ::: The code chunk below removes the unwanted column and generates a set of 4-digit HEX_ID strings along with leading zero, then converts them from character to factor (ID) type using as.factor(). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon <- hexagon %>% select(, -busstop_count) #- to drop the column hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf( "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>% #4d is to accommodate the hexagon number as.factor() #ordinal scale kable(head(hexagon)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |geometry |HEX_ID | |:------------------------------|:------| |POLYGON ((3792.538 27656.57... |H0001 | |POLYGON ((4167.538 28306.09... |H0002 | |POLYGON ((4542.538 30254.65... |H0003 | |POLYGON ((4542.538 31553.68... |H0004 | |POLYGON ((4917.538 28306.09... |H0005 | |POLYGON ((4917.538 29605.13... |H0006 | ::: ::: ## Preparing Trip Generation Data ### Cleaning the data Year_Month and destination_pt_code can be excluded from this analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # select the variables trips <- odbus %>% select (c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>% rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>% # easier when performing join later rename(HOUR_OF_DAY= TIME_PER_HOUR) %>% rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS) #easy interpration ``` ::: The BUS_STOP_N (post code of bus stop origination) is converted to factor since they are unique identifier and easier grouping group_by later. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N) kable(head(trips)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |BUS_STOP_N |DAY_TYPE | HOUR_OF_DAY| TRIPS| |:----------|:----------------|-----------:|-----:| |84671 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 9| 3| |10099 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 13| 31| |64601 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 21| 3| |53009 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 16| 10| |80051 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 18| 4| |70031 |WEEKDAY | 14| 1| ::: ::: ### Populating Hexagon IDs into BusStop data frame Next, we combine the hexagon, bus stop, and trip datasets. This code creates a lookup table linking each bus stop BUS_STOP_N to the hexagon it belongs to HEX_ID ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bs_hex <- st_intersection( BusStop, hexagon) %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID)) kable(head(bs_hex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | |BUS_STOP_N |HEX_ID | |:----|:----------|:------| |3092 |25059 |H0001 | |2439 |25751 |H0002 | |241 |26379 |H0003 | |1468 |26299 |H0004 | |2554 |25761 |H0005 | |1635 |26399 |H0006 | ::: ::: ### Adding HEX_ID into bus trips data We merge the HEX_ID and Bus Stop into trip data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips<- inner_join(trips, bs_hex) kable(head(trips)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |BUS_STOP_N |DAY_TYPE | HOUR_OF_DAY| TRIPS|HEX_ID | |:----------|:----------------|-----------:|-----:|:------| |84671 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 9| 3|H0765 | |10099 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 13| 31|H0393 | |64601 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 21| 3|H0633 | |53009 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 16| 10|H0529 | |80051 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 18| 4|H0601 | |70031 |WEEKDAY | 14| 1|H0612 | ::: ::: ### Aggregating TRIPS based on HEX_ID The code chunk below groups trip volume by **HEX_ID, DATE_TYPE, and HOUR_OF_DAY**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips <- trips %>% group_by( HEX_ID, DAY_TYPE, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) kable(head(trips)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |HEX_ID |DAY_TYPE | HOUR_OF_DAY| TRIPS| |:------|:--------|-----------:|-----:| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 6| 120| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 7| 111| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 8| 77| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 9| 66| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 10| 32| |H0001 |WEEKDAY | 11| 66| ::: ::: ### The interactive trips data frame ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} htmltools::div( # creates a html wrapper to style the table # sets font-size, 80% of page width, auto margin to center the table style = "font-size: 18px; width: 80%; margin: auto;", # makes an interactive table ((search, sort, paginate)) DT::datatable( trips, options = list( # JavaScript options pageLength = 10, # shows 10 rows per page scrollY = 500, # gives the table a 500px-tall scrollable view port scrollX = TRUE # enables horizontal scrolling ), class = "stripe hover compact" #tightens spacing ) ) ``` ::: Two more steps are required before we begin the analysis: Convert the data into a space–time cube to run EHSA on that cube.
